Saturday, 11 October 2036. Haruka Mori, 21, a Japanese violin student, arrived in Lyon two weeks ago. To get into the conservatoire, she has to pass the DELF B2 in December. She lives with Isabelle, in Odile’s flat. Rose-Hélène has come to visit.
I read newspapers without any problem. But on the radio, I hear everything and understand nothing. They speak too fast.
That’s normal. In writing, you have time. In speech, the words stick together. You have to learn to unstick them.
And they say loads of little words that are no use. “Bon”, “ben”, “du coup”, “en fait”…
They’re not useless, sweetheart. “En fait” often announces a correction. “Du coup” announces a consequence.
And in the exam, do I have to understand everything?
Certainly not. First you read the questions, you imagine what they’ll talk about, and you look for the keywords.
The hardest thing is the questions about opinion. The journalist never says “I think that”.
No, he implies it. Listen to the tone, the adjectives, the “quand même”. If someone says “well done, what a fine success” in an ironic voice, they mean the opposite.
Like Dad when I spill my hot chocolate: “Well done, champion!”
(she laughs) OK. So how do I practise?
Every day, twenty minutes of radio. First without writing anything, for the general meaning. Then a second time, noting the keywords.
And on Thursdays you come to the orchestra. Bernard Delorme talks so fast that if you understand him, you’ll understand anyone.
And if he talks about the trumpet, at least I’ll understand one word.
(“les uns aux autres” = to one another)
“J’sais pas” = “shay-pa”: in fast speech, “je” shrinks to “j” and blends in.
“Samedi” = “sam-dee”: the silent “e” disappears in everyday speech.
The paper lasts about 30 minutes and is marked out of 25. You listen to authentic documents (interviews, broadcasts, reports, lectures):
understand the main ideas, details, opinions
You have time to read the questions BEFORE the first listening. Use it! Underline the keywords in the questions.
Anticipate: read the title and the questions. What will it be about?
First listening: the general meaning (who? what? why?).
Never leave a question unanswered (no points are deducted for wrong answers).
Typical mistake: getting stuck on an unknown word. Keep going! The general meaning matters more than one word.
The “little” words show you the structure of what is said:
En fait, ce n’est pas si simple.
Il pleuvait, du coup on est restés.
DELF questions often ask you to identify the speaker’s attitude. Signs of opinion:
The festival welcomed 20,000 visitors. (FACT: verifiable figure)
The festival was a remarkable success. (OPINION: evaluative adjective)
It is regrettable that prices are so high. (OPINION: verb of feeling)
Apparently the mayor is going to resign. (RUMOUR: uncertain information)
Watch out for the conditional in the press: “Le maire aurait démissionné” = UNCONFIRMED information (“reportedly resigned”).
At B2 you must understand what is NOT said directly:
Irony: it means the opposite (“how clumsy you are”).
Litotes: it means “the film is poor”.
Implied: “you’re late” or “it’s late, go to bed”.
Tone of voice is the key to irony. Listen to where the voice rises and falls: exaggerated intonation often signals irony.

Elle ne comprend pas la radio
Quand Haruka passe-t-elle le DELF B2 ?
Combien de temps Haruka doit-elle écouter la radio chaque jour ?
“Ce n’est pas le film du siècle” means…

Haruka Mori was twenty-one, and she had arrived in Lyon on Saturday 27 September 2036, with a suitcase, a rucksack and a violin case she never let go of. In the case was Gérard Thiébaut’s hundred-and-fiftieth violin, the one he had given her ten months earlier, on the night of the film premiere, in the foyer of the Institut Lumière. She had cried when she received it. She had decided that evening that she would come back to Lyon for good.

She came from Kyoto. She had played the violin since the age of four, thanks to her grandmother, who had been a music teacher at a secondary school for forty years. She had discovered the waltz on the internet, like millions of people, watching the video of the silence on the Place des Terreaux. She had learnt it by heart in one evening. Then she had played it for her grandmother, who fell silent at the right moment without anyone explaining it to her.

At the premiere she had come with her friend Aoi, a musicology student who had discovered the waltz at the same time as she had. Aoi had stayed in Japan. She had founded a waltz club at Kyoto University, which already had sixty members. They met on Friday evenings in a lecture room and observed the silence of the third verse with a discipline the Lyonnais had never known. Aoi sent videos every week.

Her dream was to get into the Lyon conservatoire, in the violin class. She had taken the audition in June, by video, and been admitted. But there was one condition: to present a B2-level French diploma before January. The DELF B2. Without it, no enrolment. Haruka had studied French for three years at Kyoto University. She read Camus and Saint-Exupéry in the original. She thought it would be easy.

Her plane had landed at Saint-Exupéry airport. Haruka had found that funny: she had read “The Little Prince” three times, and it was the first French word she saw on arrival. Then she had taken a taxi. The driver talked to her the whole way, with great enthusiasm, about football, the weather and his brother-in-law. Haruka understood only the name of the Lyon team. She nodded for forty minutes. The driver found her charming.

It was Isabelle who had offered to put her up. She lived alone in Odile’s flat, rue d’Austerlitz, since her children had left, and there was a spare room, the one Isabelle had slept in as a child. She had told Haruka on the phone that the room was small, the parquet creaked, and the neighbour opposite, a certain Rose-Hélène, would probably knock on her door every day. Haruka had said it was perfect.

On the first evening, Isabelle showed her round the flat. Odile’s armchair had come back from the museum and was back in its place by the window, with the blue shawl over the back. On the living-room wall hung the old photo of Henri, a young sailor, smiling, with his harmonica. Isabelle told her the whole story, slowly, choosing simple words. Haruka understood everything, because Isabelle spoke the way you speak to someone you really want to see understand.

The first days were a disaster. On Sunday morning at the bakery, the baker asked her something very fast, with a big smile. Haruka didn’t recognise a single word. She answered “yes”. The baker gave her a baguette, two croissants, an apple tart and a newspaper. Haruka paid without a word, red with shame. Isabelle laughed when she saw breakfast for six arriving. She said the baker had only asked: “Anything else?”

At the supermarket on Monday, the cashier asked her a very short question. Haruka said “no”. The cashier asked another. Haruka said “no” again, to be safe. At the third she said “no” one last time. She found out later that the cashier had asked whether she had a loyalty card, whether she wanted a bag, and whether she wanted her receipt. She had left with no card, no bag and no receipt, her shopping in her arms.

On the bus, Haruka couldn’t understand the announcements. In the street, she couldn’t understand people asking her the way, which happened often, because she looked as if she knew where she was going. On the phone it was even worse: without lips, without gestures, the voice came through like a continuous noise, a river of sounds without spaces. She felt as if she were deaf. She, who had perfect pitch and could recognise an A to within two hertz.

There was also the question of the bise. In Japan you didn’t touch each other to say hello. In Lyon, everyone kissed her on both cheeks, even people she was meeting for the first time. She never knew which side to start on. On the first Thursday she bumped noses with Bernard Delorme. Isabelle explained that in Lyon people gave two kisses, in Montpellier three, and in Brittany sometimes four. Haruka noted that in her notebook, with a diagram.

On Wednesday she had to phone the prefecture about her residence permit. A man’s voice gave her an appointment. Haruka carefully wrote down: “the sixteenth, at ten o’clock”. The following Monday she turned up at the prefecture at ten, file under her arm. She was told her appointment was on the twenty-sixth, at five in the afternoon. She had confused “seize” and “vingt-six”, “dix heures” and “dix-sept heures”. She walked home crying in the rain.

At the conservatoire, the secretary had reeled off the list of documents needed for enrolment at top speed. Haruka had only caught the end: “… and the DELF B2 before 15 January, otherwise we can’t do anything for you.” She asked politely whether the secretary could repeat it more slowly. The secretary repeated it at exactly the same speed, but louder. Haruka understood that day that speaking louder was the French people’s universal solution when faced with foreigners.

That evening Rose-Hélène knocked on the door, as Isabelle had predicted. She was eight and a half and had come to see whether the Japanese girl really played Mr Thiébaut’s violin. She found Haruka sitting on her bed, red-eyed, surrounded by sheets of paper on which she had written the French numbers in big letters. Rose-Hélène looked at the sheets. Then she said, very seriously, that French numbers were the silliest thing in the world, and that even the French knew it.

She explained that “soixante-dix-sept” meant “sixty plus ten plus seven”, and “quatre-vingt-dix-neuf” meant “four times twenty plus ten plus nine”. She said the Belgians and the Swiss said “septante” and “nonante”, like normal people, and she thought that was much better. Haruka laughed in spite of herself. Rose-Hélène said that was a start. Then she asked whether she could see the violin.

Haruka opened the case. Rose-Hélène looked at the violin for a long time without touching it, respectfully. Then she took her harmonica out of her pocket and played the first three notes of the waltz. Haruka picked up the violin, put it under her chin and played the next three notes. Then the rest. Then the whole waltz, up to the silence, where they both stopped together without looking at each other. For the first time since she arrived, Haruka had understood everything.

On Saturday, Isabelle took her to the Croix-Rousse market on the boulevard. The stallholders shouted their prices, joked with customers, called out to passers-by. Haruka understood nothing, but she loved the noise. At a cheese stall she asked, very slowly, a sentence she had practised ten times: “Excuse me, could you repeat that more slowly, please?” The cheesemonger repeated it very slowly. Then he let her taste three cheeses. She understood everything.

The next evening Isabelle took Haruka to the Thursday orchestra. It was her third week in Lyon. She was terrified. Forty people all talking at once, fast, laughing, with expressions she had never read in any book. Bernard Delorme especially. He talked faster than anyone, with a Lyon accent you could cut with a knife, and he peppered every sentence with “ben”, “hein” and “quand même”. Haruka didn’t understand a word he said to her.

But when Théo raised his baton and the orchestra began to play, everything became clear. Music she understood. She sat next to Bertrand in the second row of violins and played Sorina’s Romanian dance, sight-reading the score for the first time, without a single wrong note. Bertrand looked at her with admiration. He told Amina at the break that he had never heard anyone play like that in that hall.

Then came the waltz. Haruka knew it by heart. At the third verse, when the whole orchestra fell silent, she fell silent too. Eight bars. On the fifth, Amina struck her triangle. Then Bernard Delorme sounded his foghorn, the one he had bought for Yves, and Haruka jumped so hard she nearly dropped her violin. The whole hall burst out laughing. So did Haruka. She hadn’t understood the words. But she had understood the joke.

After rehearsal, Mr Haddad, who now came every Thursday to play the oud in the orchestra, came up to her. He told her slowly that he had lived in France for twenty years and still didn’t understand Bernard Delorme. Haruka laughed. Mr Haddad added that at first he hadn’t understood the radio either. He had learnt French by listening to the same news every evening at the same time. He said repetition was the mother of all languages.

On the way home that evening, Isabelle explained her method. She had been a publisher in Paris for thirty years, had worked with translators from all over the world, and knew how you learnt a language by ear. Twenty minutes of radio every day. No more, no less. The first time without writing anything, just for the general meaning. The second time noting the keywords. And above all, never stopping on a word you don’t understand.

Haruka asked why. Isabelle answered with a comparison Haruka never forgot. She said understanding a language was like following a melody. If you stopped at every note you didn’t know, you lost the whole piece. You had to follow the thread, accept that you wouldn’t hear everything, and trust what came next. Haruka said she knew how to do that with a violin. Isabelle said: “Then do it with your ears.”

The next morning Haruka began. She sat in Odile’s kitchen with a bowl of green tea, a radio and a notebook. Twenty minutes. The first time she understood nothing except a few isolated words: “government”, “rain”, “Lyon”. The second time she noted twelve words. She looked them up in the dictionary. The third time she understood it was about a transport strike, caused by works on the lines. She was very proud.

The next day, Gérard Thiébaut phoned from Mirecourt to ask how his violin was doing. He was eighty-three and spoke slowly, with a Vosges accent, articulating every syllable. Haruka understood every word. She was so surprised that she told him so. The old luthier laughed. He said it was a well-known secret: old people spoke slowly because they had all the time in the world. He advised her to talk to old people a lot before talking to young ones.

Then she told Isabelle what she had understood. Isabelle listened to the end, then said gently that it wasn’t a strike. It was a report on a music festival that had had to be cancelled because of the rain, and the word “strike” didn’t appear anywhere. Haruka’s face fell. Isabelle laughed. She said it didn’t matter: she had understood “Lyon”, “rain” and “cancelled”. In the exam, that would already have earned her two points.

Haruka took the advice. She started listening to podcasts on the bus every morning on the way to her preparation classes. One morning she was so absorbed in an interview that she missed her stop. Then the next one. She ended up at the terminus, in Vaulx-en-Velin, on the other side of the city. The driver asked whether she was all right. She answered that she had understood the whole interview. The driver couldn’t understand why she looked so happy.

Everyone in the building started helping Haruka, each in their own way. Rose-Hélène made her watch cartoons on Wednesday afternoons, because the characters spoke slowly and repeated everything three times. Henri-Ion, who was five, talked to her non-stop, about everything and nothing, dinosaurs, sailors’ knots and his friend Lucas, and never gave her time to answer. Haruka said it was the best practice possible: a native speaker who never stopped.

Inès, who was preparing her own law exams, explained the traps of the paper. Multiple-choice questions, where two answers seem right. “True or false”, where you have to justify by copying a precise sentence from the document. Short answers, where you mustn’t write a novel. She told her never to leave a box empty, because you didn’t lose points for a wrong answer. Haruka wrote: “Always answer. Like the waltz.”

Julien lent her French films with French subtitles. Not Japanese, he insisted. French. So she could see the words while hearing them. They watched them together on Sunday evenings, nineties comedies where everyone shouted. Haruka didn’t always understand why people laughed. Julien explained the puns. She said humour was the last thing you understood in a foreign language.

Léonie Garnier invited her one evening to watch “Répondre” at her place, with French subtitles. Haruka had seen the film at the cinema, at the premiere, without understanding the dialogue. This time she understood Odile’s sentences, Bernard’s jokes, Bertrand’s silences. When the screen went black in the middle of the film, she didn’t need subtitles. She whistled the three notes at the end of the eighth second. Léonie said it was the most beautiful translation of the film she knew.

Sami, who often came to the rue d’Austerlitz now that he was studying literature, taught her something else. He made her listen to rap songs with the lyrics in front of her. He showed her how words swallowed one another: “je suis” becoming “chuis”, “il y a” becoming “y a”, “tu es” becoming “t’es”. Haruka filled three pages of her notebook with these transformations. She said it was like a second language hidden inside the first.

On 1 November, All Saints’ Day, Isabelle took her to the Croix-Rousse cemetery, to Odile and Henri’s grave. They brought chrysanthemums, like all the French on that day. Haruka said that in Japan there was a similar festival in summer, Obon, when the spirits of the dead are welcomed into the home. Isabelle said it was a beautiful idea. They stood for a moment in silence in front of the grave. Then Haruka played the waltz on the violin, very softly, among the graves.

But it was Ioana who helped her most. One October evening, Haruka was sitting on the first step of the stairs, on the landing, with her earphones in, crying silently. She had just listened to a ten-minute interview and understood nothing. Ioana, coming home from work, sat down beside her. She didn’t ask anything. She just said that ten years ago she had sat in exactly the same place, for exactly the same reason.

She told her about her arrival in Lyon in 2026. A young Romanian architect who had learnt French from books, like Haruka, and understood nothing when people spoke to her. Who confused “poisson” and “poison”, “cheveux” and “chevaux”. Who felt so lonely some evenings that she wanted to get back on the plane. And then one evening, on this landing, an old lady had whistled three notes on the other side of the door. Ioana had answered. Everything had begun there.

Haruka asked how long it had taken her to really understand. Ioana thought about it. She said: six months for the radio, a year for jokes, two years for arguments, and ten years for Lyonnais talking with their mouths full. Haruka laughed through her tears. Ioana added that after three months, one morning, without knowing why, she had understood an entire radio column from beginning to end. As if someone had opened a window.

From that evening on, Ioana got into the habit of spending half an hour with Haruka, twice a week, on the landing. They sat on the first step. Ioana played her a three-minute document, then asked her questions, as in the exam. Who is speaking? About what? What is their opinion? How do you know? Haruka answered in French, slowly. Ioana corrected her in Romanian when she was tired, which made Haruka laugh, since she didn’t understand a word of Romanian.

One Thursday at the break, Théo asked her how you said “silence” in Japanese. Haruka thought about it. She said there was a word, “ma”, that didn’t exactly mean silence. It meant the space between things. The interval between two notes, between two words, between two people. An emptiness that wasn’t empty, because it gave meaning to what surrounded it. Théo was silent for a long time. Then he said that was exactly what the waltz had been doing for fifty years.

The hardest thing for Haruka was the questions about opinion. In Japan you never said directly what you thought. You let people guess. She should have been at ease with innuendo. But French innuendo was different from Japanese innuendo. In Japanese you hinted out of politeness. In French you often hinted out of irony. Someone would say “that’s brilliant” and mean “that’s rubbish”. Haruka found that very rude. And very difficult.

Ioana taught her to listen to the tone rather than the words. She made her listen to the same sentence said three different ways: “What a lovely day.” Sincere, ironic, tired. At first Haruka heard no difference. After two weeks she recognised two out of three. After a month she could recognise Julien’s irony from ten metres away through a closed door. Julien said that was worrying. Ioana said it was progress.

One evening Sorina called from Bucharest by video and introduced Haruka to Viorica, who was ninety-six. Viorica spoke the French of another century, learnt in her youth, full of imperfect subjunctives and old-fashioned formulas. She articulated every word like a pearl. Haruka understood everything. Viorica told her she spoke French better than most French people, which was untrue. Then she played the three notes on the piano with one finger, and Haruka answered on the violin.

At the end of October, Haruka took a mock exam at the Alliance française in Lyon, under real conditions. A classroom, thirty candidates, a teacher handing out the papers, loudspeakers in the ceiling. The first document was an interview with a sociologist about remote working, played twice. The others were radio news items, played once. Haruka’s throat was dry and her hands were clammy. She got eleven out of twenty-five.

You needed at least five not to be eliminated, and fifty out of a hundred in total to pass. Eleven wasn’t a disaster. But for Haruka, who had always been top of her class, it was a humiliation. She went back to the rue d’Austerlitz without a word. She shut herself in her room. She didn’t play the violin that evening. Isabelle knocked on the door. Haruka didn’t answer. It was the first time.

Around ten that evening, Haruka heard something on the other side of her door. Not knocking. Three notes. Whistled, off-key, very off-key. It wasn’t Isabelle, nor Rose-Hélène, who had been asleep for ages. It was Henri-Ion, who had got up in his pyjamas, crossed the landing without telling anyone and was whistling outside her door, with his five years and his baby teeth. He didn’t know why Haruka was sad. He only knew that someone had to answer.

Haruka opened her door. Henri-Ion stood there, barefoot, his hair sticking up. He told her, very fast, a sentence she understood completely, first time, without effort: “You’re sad ’cause you failed your exam, but it doesn’t matter, I fail all the time too, and then I pass.” Haruka knelt down and hugged him. Then she realised something: she had understood “t’es”, “t’as” and “c’est pas” without thinking.

That night, for the first time, Haruka dreamt in French. It was a confused dream, in which Bernard Delorme sold croissants on the bus and the prefecture gave her an appointment at seventy-seven o’clock. She didn’t understand everything people said to her in the dream. But she answered them in French, without thinking. When she woke up she told Isabelle. Isabelle said it was an excellent sign: when you dream in a language, it means it is beginning to live inside you.

The next day she started again. Twenty minutes of radio. Three minutes with Ioana on the landing. Cartoons with Rose-Hélène. Henri-Ion’s monologues. Sami’s songs. Julien’s films. And on Thursdays, Bernard Delorme, who had become, without knowing it, her hardest and therefore most useful test. Every evening she wrote in her notebook the words she had understood from him. The first week there were four. The third, forty.

At the beginning of November a parcel arrived from Kyoto. Haruka’s grandmother had sent it. Inside there was green tea, rice cakes and about a hundred folded paper cranes of every colour. A letter in Japanese explained that one crane was for Haruka, and all the others were for the people helping her in Lyon. Haruka gave one to each of them. Rose-Hélène hung hers above her bed, next to her three keys.

One Thursday in November, at the break, Bernard Delorme told her a long story about the Vénissieux brass band in 1975, his uniform that was too small and a concert in the snow during which the tuba player lost his false teeth inside his instrument. He told it at full speed, with his accent, his “hein” and his “ben”, laughing himself before the punchline. Haruka burst out laughing at the right moment. Bernard stopped, surprised. He said: “Well I never, she understands me!”

The whole hall applauded. Monique, Bernard’s wife, who had come to listen to the rehearsal, said it was a miracle, because she herself hadn’t understood him for fifty years. Bernard pretended to be offended. Then he gave Haruka an old record of the Vénissieux brass band, on vinyl, which she had no way of playing. She hung it on her bedroom wall in Odile’s flat, next to the window. She said it was her first French diploma.

One day Sami brought her the text of his slam, “Eight Bars”, printed on four pages. He asked her to read it aloud. Haruka stumbled over the verlan, laughed with the sailor, understood Odile first time and tripped over every one of the prefect’s sentences. Sami said that was exactly the order of difficulty for a French person too. Then he told her that in the oral exam she wouldn’t need either the verlan or the prefect. Just Odile. Everyday French.

In the evenings, when she was homesick, Haruka called her grandmother in Kyoto. With the time difference, it was morning there. Her grandmother was eighty-three and didn’t speak a word of French, but she always asked about the waltz. Haruka told her about the orchestra, Bernard, the foghorn, Rose-Hélène’s cartoons. One evening her grandmother asked her to say something in French. Anything. Just to hear it.

Haruka thought about it. Then she said Odile’s sentence, the one written on the museum wall: “If one day you hear whistling on the other side of the landing, don’t look for who it is. Answer.” Her grandmother listened in silence. Then she said, in Japanese, that it was a very beautiful language, and that she had understood. Haruka asked how she could have understood without speaking French. Her grandmother said: “I heard the music. The meaning was inside it.”

On Sundays Amina and Bertrand often came to lunch at the rue d’Austerlitz with Awa, who was five months old and starting to babble. She made “ba”, “da” and “mmm” sounds, watching the adults with intense concentration. Haruka watched her with great interest. She said she and Awa were in the same situation: they heard everything, understood very little, and tried anyway. Amina said she had made a spreadsheet to compare their progress.

The spreadsheet had two columns, “Awa” and “Haruka”, and one row per week. In Awa’s column there were things like “smiles when her name is said” or “turns at the sound of the triangle”. In Haruka’s: “understands the baker”, “understands the bus announcements”, “laughs at one of Bernard’s jokes”. Amina said that at this rate Awa would say her first word at about the time Haruka took her exam. Haruka said it was a race. She intended to win.

Little by little, Haruka began to answer the phone without panicking. She called the prefecture back on her own to confirm her new appointment, and understood the date first time: the twenty-sixth, at five in the afternoon. She even dared ask the voice on the line to repeat the file number, which she would never have done a month earlier. The voice repeated it. More slowly this time, and not louder. Haruka thought it was great progress for the prefecture.

One morning at the end of November, Haruka switched on the radio as usual, with her bowl of green tea, in Odile’s kitchen. It was a column. The columnist’s voice sounded familiar. It was the one who had criticised Sami’s slam in the spring. He was talking about the French language, how it was evolving, and quoting new words. Then he came to the word “ouf”. Haruka put down her bowl. She listened without breathing.

The columnist told the history of the word, its verlan origin, its entry into young people’s language. Then, at the end, in a perfectly serious voice, he said you had to beware of this word, because it was contagious: he had heard it that very morning from his own mother, aged ninety, who had learnt it from her great-grandson. He concluded: “If even my mother says ouf, the French language is not about to die.”

Haruka burst out laughing. Alone in the kitchen at eight in the morning. She had understood everything. The words, the structure, and above all the tone: the gentle irony, the self-mockery, the tenderness hidden beneath the seriousness. She had understood that the columnist was making fun of himself. That he was answering Sami without naming him. That this was his way of apologising. She had understood what he didn’t say. For the first time she had heard a foreign language the way you hear music.

She ran onto the landing in her pyjamas. She knocked on the door opposite, Julien and Ioana’s. Ioana opened it, a cup of coffee in her hand, still half asleep. Haruka told her everything at once, in French, very fast, without searching for words, with “en fait”, “du coup” and a “c’est ouf” at the end. Ioana listened to the end. Then she smiled. She said: “There. The window has opened.”

The night before the second mock exam, Isabelle gave her an old pencil with a chewed end. It was the pencil Odile used to write her shopping lists with, the one that had drawn a little musical note at the bottom of one of them. Isabelle said she didn’t believe in lucky charms. But Odile did, very much, and it couldn’t do any harm. Haruka slept with the pencil under her pillow, as Sami had with his notebooks.

The second mock exam took place the following week at the Alliance française, in the same room, with the same loudspeakers in the ceiling. The first document was a lecture on protecting the oceans. Haruka read the questions before listening, underlined the keywords, and imagined what it would be about. During the first listening she wrote nothing. During the second she noted twelve words. She didn’t panic once. She got nineteen out of twenty-five.

Leaving the Alliance française, she called her grandmother in Kyoto, even though it was very late there. She told her the result in Japanese, then repeated the sentence in French, for the pleasure of it. Her grandmother didn’t understand the French numbers, but she understood her granddaughter’s voice. She said it was the first time in two months that Haruka sounded as if she lived in Lyon, and not just stayed there. Haruka said that was exactly it.

That evening at the Thursday rehearsal she announced her result to the whole orchestra. Bernard Delorme sounded his foghorn, which set off the hall’s alarm. Amina added a row to the spreadsheet: “Haruka: 19 out of 25”. Opposite, in Awa’s column, she wrote: “Awa: said ‘ba’ looking at Haruka.” Everyone decided it was a draw. Théo raised his baton. They played the waltz.

After rehearsal, Ioana reminded her that listening comprehension was only one of the four papers. There was still reading comprehension, written production and oral production, each marked out of twenty-five. She had three weeks left before the exam, set for Saturday 13 December. Haruka asked which was the hardest. Ioana thought about it. She said that for her it had been the oral. Because you could learn to understand on your own. But to speak, you needed someone opposite you who listened.

That evening, coming back to the rue d’Austerlitz, Haruka stopped on the landing. It was late. The whole building was asleep. Behind the door opposite there was no sound. Haruka thought of Ioana, sitting on the same step ten years earlier, lost in a language she didn’t understand. Of Odile, who had whistled for her. She took her violin out of its case. Very softly, so as not to wake anyone, she played three notes. And on the other side of the door, someone answered.

Reading: Transcript of a radio column

The transcript of a radio column about language learning, as in the listening paper. Notice the spoken markers, the facts and the opinions. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Chronique : « Apprendre une langue à l’oreille »

Hello everyone. So, today we’re talking about a problem everyone learning a language knows: you can read without difficulty, but when it comes to speech, you’re lost. According to a recent study, seven foreign students out of ten say the same thing.

Why? Well, actually, it’s quite simple. In writing, words are separated by spaces. In speech, they stick together: people don’t say “je ne sais pas”, they say “chais pas”. As a result, the ear no longer recognises words it actually knows.

Specialists recommend a surprisingly simple method: listen every day, even a little, even without understanding everything. Twenty minutes would apparently be enough. OK, twenty minutes is still easier said than done.

Another tip: don’t be afraid of the unknown. Anyone who stops at every word they don’t understand ends up understanding nothing at all. It’s better to follow the thread, the way you follow a melody without knowing all the notes.

And then there are the “little words”: bon, ben, enfin, bref. Some teachers consider them useless. Not at all, in my view. They’re signposts: they announce a conclusion, a correction, a change of subject.
In short, if you don’t understand the radio, don’t worry: you’re not alone. And if you understand this column to the end, well… you’re on the right track. Until next week!
